briefing.question: Loyalty versus conscience: when does keeping faith with a group become complicity, and when does breaking with it become betrayal?
briefing.agreed: A pledge and a conscience both bind; neither label settles it.
briefing.split: Aquinas, a formed conscience; Kant, Cicero, the pledge; Burke, fight within; Washington, Thoreau.

briefing.question: Law versus legitimacy: can something be lawful and still corrupt the consent of the governed, and who gets to police it without corrupting it further?
briefing.agreed: Lawful acts can corrupt consent; no interested party should police it.
briefing.split: Aristotle, equity by a fit judge; Cicero, chicanery; Locke, the people; Hamilton; Madison.

briefing.question: Order versus liberty in the franchise: is it worse to count one ineligible vote or to block one eligible voter?
briefing.agreed: Only citizens vote; no citizen loses a ballot on suspicion.
briefing.split: Blackstone, Beccaria, proof first; Hobbes, enforce to protect; Locke, the states; Madison.

briefing.question: What does each generation owe the next, and what are the limits of legitimate protest when the social contract feels broken?
briefing.agreed: The young have a real claim; violence is not a form of it.
briefing.split: Burke, reform; Rousseau, consent anew; Locke, long abuses; Hobbes, order; King; Mill, incitement.

briefing.question: The dignity of the poor: can you portray suffering without exploiting it, and does intent excuse effect?
briefing.agreed: Portrayal must point to the sufferer, not the portrayer.
briefing.split: Smith, neglect of the poor; Kant, intent and means; Mill, effects; Aristotle, tact; Bakhtin.

briefing.question: Should society bend to the sun or the sun's hours to society? Popular preference versus hard-won experience.
briefing.agreed: The clock should serve life; weigh past experiments first.
briefing.split: Franklin, habits; Chesterton, the fence; Burke, preserve; Plato, experts; Aristotle, both.

briefing.question: Faith in public life: when the state funds a service, can it require religious providers to act against their convictions, and can religious providers take public money while declining to serve some families?
briefing.agreed: The state may not buy doctrine; no child is lesser.
briefing.split: Madison, both ways; Leo XIII, family and plural schools; Mill, fund not run; Aquinas; Locke.

briefing.question: Church and state: is the pulpit a place of prophetic witness on public life, or should faith communities keep a distance from partisan power to protect both the church and the republic?
briefing.agreed: The pulpit speaks to morals; party ties harm the church.
briefing.split: Williams, wall from inside; Augustine, two cities; Ambrose, confront; Tocqueville; Leo XIII.

briefing.question: Unity versus purity, and authority versus autonomy: what holds a church together, and who owns a sacred inheritance?
briefing.agreed: A church is more than its members; part with patience.
briefing.split: Wesley, love across difference; Augustine, unity; Cyprian, bishop; Locke, consent; Burke, trust.

briefing.question: Peace versus justice: is any ceasefire a moral good, or can peace without justice entrench a wrong?
briefing.agreed: Saving civilians is good; a truce is not yet a just peace.
briefing.split: Augustine, just order; Aquinas, evil peace; Erasmus, any peace; Kant, truce; Thucydides, power.

setup.text: A Michigan congresswoman who lost the August Democratic primary for Senate, and then endorsed the winner, switched on Sunday to back the Republican nominee after being asked to stay away from a joint Detroit event. sittings.why_these_chairs: Aquinas speaks first because the report names his teaching on the correct and the erring conscience, the fullest classical account of when conscience binds and when it can be wrong. Kant is named for promise-keeping as a duty in itself, and his Groundwork uses the false promise as its first worked example. Burke wrote the classic defense of party as a body of men united on principle; Washington's Farewell Address is the classic warning against the spirit of party, and the report sets the two against each other. Thoreau is named for the individual conscience against the collective. Cicero is added because De Officiis states both that good faith is the foundation of justice and that some promises should not be kept, the exact tension of the night. Machiavelli, who wrote that a prince need not keep faith when it turns against him, is left off because his advice is about rulers' advantage, not a member's duty to a party. The congresswoman, the nominees and party leaders are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: loyalty versus conscience. When does keeping faith with a group become complicity, and when does breaking with it become betrayal? The report gives one side as saying conscience outranks party: if she believes her party's nominee has tolerated antisemitism and shut her out, she owes voters her honest judgment, and she says she is not turning her back on Democrats. The other side says a primary is a promise: you compete, you lose, you back the winner, and breaking that pledge two days before an election that could decide Senate control is sour grapes dressed up as principle. We decide nothing tonight about the ad or the candidates. Aquinas, you begin.

chairs.name: Thomas Aquinas

turn.text: The report names my question on the erring conscience, so let me give both halves of it. First, conscience binds even when it is mistaken. I concluded that “every will at variance with reason, whether right or erring, is always evil” (Summa Theologica I-II, Q. 19, Art. 5) A person who truly judges that staying silent would make her complicit in a wrong may not simply override that judgment to keep a pledge. To act against one's conscience is always a fault.

turn.text: But the second half matters as much. A conscience can err, and not every error excuses. “But if the error arise from ignorance of some circumstance, and without any negligence, so that it cause the act to be involuntary, then that error of reason or conscience excuses the will, that abides by that erring reason, from being evil.” (Summa Theologica I-II, Q. 19, Art. 6) The error that excuses is the honest one about facts that could not be known. An error that comes from negligence, from not looking hard at the facts, or from letting resentment pass itself off as judgment, does not excuse. So I would ask her, and her critics, the same thing: has the conscience been formed with care, or is it only following the injury?

turn.text: Aquinas begins inside the conscience; I begin with the promise, because that is the critics' charge. In my first example I asked: “May I when in distress make a promise with the intention not to keep it?” (Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section) The answer is no, and the reason is not the consequences. If everyone pledged support after losing and withdrew it whenever convenient, the pledge would mean nothing. “Hence my maxim, as soon as it should be made a universal law, would necessarily destroy itself.” (Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section)

A promise binds the one who makes it, but it cannot oblige anyone to do wrong; a duty to keep faith gives way only to a stricter duty, never to an inclination. If it would, the pledge does not bind. If she cannot name such a duty, the pledge stands, whatever it costs her.

A pledge can give way only to a stricter moral duty, not to personal feelings, so the real question is whether keeping it would require doing something wrong.

That makes loyalty important, but loyalty is owed to the shared principle, so someone who leaves should first fight from within and then explain exactly which principle was abandoned.

turn.text: Burke praises the party; I spent my last public words warning against its spirit. I wished to “warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party, generally.” (Farewell Address (1796)) The danger I saw was that party loyalty would replace loyalty to the country, and that each side would come to see the other as the enemy. “The alternate domination of one faction over another, sharpened by the spirit of revenge, natural to party dissension, which in different ages and countries has perpetrated the most horrid enormities, is itself a frightful despotism.” (Farewell Address (1796))

sittings.why_these_chairs: Blackstone speaks first because the report names his ratio, that it is better ten guilty escape than one innocent suffer, and because he also wrote that a free state must regulate who may vote, so both sides can cite him. Beccaria wrote on presumption of innocence and on preventing harms rather than punishing them, the two halves of the dispute over setting ballots aside. Swift, the great satirist of the rich and the poor, is left off because his Modest Proposal is satire aimed at the powerful, a different case from a costume. sittings.question: Should society bend to the sun or the sun's hours to society? Popular preference versus hard-won experience.

setup.text: Americans turned their clocks back an hour on Sunday. sittings.why_these_chairs: Benjamin Franklin speaks first because he wrote the most famous essay on fitting human hours to sunlight, a satirical letter of 1784 often credited as the idea behind daylight saving. G. K. Chesterton is named for his fence, the rule not to remove a custom until you know why it was put up; the passage is in The Thing (1929) and is given in paraphrase only. Burke wrote that a statesman should combine a disposition to preserve with an ability to improve. Plato is named for the case for expert rulers against majority preference; his ship of state image even names the seasons and the sky. Aristotle answered Plato that the many together may judge better than the few. Ecclesiastes enters through the moderator. The senators, the president and sleep-health groups are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: should society bend to the sun, or the sun's hours to society? Popular preference against hard-won experience. The Preacher said: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecclesiastes 3:1) The report gives one side as saying people want evening light for family, commerce and safety, and that switching twice a year is pointless disruption. The other side, including sleep-health advocates and a leading senator, says permanent daylight saving time has been tried and repealed before because of pitch-dark winter mornings and children walking to school in the dark, and that if the switching ends, it should end on standard time, closer to the body's natural clock. Franklin, you begin.

turn.text: Notice what I actually proposed. I did not move the clock; I moved the people, with taxes on shutters and church bells at sunrise. And I anticipated tonight's objection: “If it should be said, that people are apt to be obstinately attached to old customs, and that it will be difficult to induce them to rise before noon, consequently my discovery can be of little use: I answer, Nil desperandum.” (An Economical Project (letter to the Journal de Paris, 1784)) I was teasing the Parisians for sleeping past noon. The joke cuts both ways tonight: those who want evening light want the sun on their schedule, and those who want standard time want people back on the sun's. My serious point is that habits, not clocks, decide how much daylight we use.

sittings.question: Faith in public life: when the state funds a service, can it require religious providers to act against their convictions, and can religious providers take public money while declining to serve some families?

sittings.why_these_chairs: Madison speaks first because the report names his Memorial and Remonstrance, which defends conscience and also objects to taxing citizens for religious teaching. Pope Leo XIII speaks for the Catholic social teaching the report names, on the family's prior right in education. Mill made the liberal case for funding schools without running them. Aquinas grounds parental custody in natural justice. Locke limits law to civil ends. The court cases the report names enter as context, not chairs, and the archdiocese, state, families and justices are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: faith in public life. When the state funds a service, can it require religious providers to act against their convictions, and can religious providers take public money while declining to serve some families? The report gives one side, the preschools, as saying they want only the same accommodation other providers get, that a recent precedent bars a state from excluding schools because of their religious exercise, and that dropping church teaching on marriage and sex has been made the price of admission. The other side, Colorado, says the schools remain welcome on the same equal-opportunity terms as every publicly funded preschool, religious or secular, and that taxpayer money should not fund a program that can turn away a child because of who the child's parents are. We predict no ruling. Madison, you begin.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Roger Williams speaks first because the report names his wall built to protect the garden of the church from the wilderness of the world, the original argument that separation protects religion. Augustine is named for the two cities. Ambrose is added for the prophetic tradition the report names: he refused communion to an emperor until he repented, a pulpit confronting power without endorsing a faction. Tocqueville observed that American religion was strong precisely because it stayed out of party politics. Pope Leo XIII wrote in Sapientiae Christianae that the Church must not be tied to any party, while Christians must act in public life. Nathan before David enters through the moderator. The abolitionist and civil-rights preachers the report names are honored in the closing but not seated, since their sermons are largely in copyright or not available as verified texts tonight. The pastor, the candidates, the party committees and the advocacy groups are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: church and state. Is the pulpit a place of prophetic witness on public life, or should faith communities keep a distance from partisan power to protect both the church and the republic? The report recalls the prophet before the king: “And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7) It gives one side, the pastor and his allies, as saying the restriction is unconstitutional censorship of political speech, that pastors have preached on public questions since the founding, and that churches earn their tax status through social work. The other side, including a party committee and secular groups, says tax-exempt status is a public subsidy that should not underwrite partisan campaigns, and that mixing pulpit and party corrupts both. We settle no court case tonight. Williams, you begin.

sittings.why_these_chairs: John Wesley speaks first because he founded Methodism and preached the Catholic Spirit sermon on how Christians who cannot think alike may still love alike, and on why that is not indifference. Augustine is named for his long fight against the Donatists over whether a mixed church should stay united; his City of God passage on the two cities intermixed until judgment states the principle. Cyprian wrote On the Unity of the Church, the classic text for the connectional, episcopal side. Locke defined a church as a voluntary society, the classic case for congregational autonomy. Burke is named for an inheritance held in trust for those who come after. Calvin and the Reformation's congregational thinkers are left off because the report names the debate but no particular text of theirs. The congregations, the bishop and the conference are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: unity versus purity, and authority versus autonomy. What holds a church together, and who owns a sacred inheritance? The report gives one side, those who left, as saying a congregation that overwhelmingly votes its conscience should be free to chart its own course and keep the church it built. The other side, those who stayed and the conference, says a Methodist church belongs to a connectional covenant larger than any one generation of members, so the bishop's authority and the denomination's claim to the property still stand. We decide no property question tonight. Wesley, you begin.

Erasmus is added because his Complaint of Peace makes the strongest case that almost any peace is better than war, the supporters' side in its purest form. Thucydides is named for the Melian Dialogue, the realist's account of what the strong and the weak may expect.
